region: Laboratory and field, southern Rocky Mountains (Colorado)
quote: These data suggest that cutthroat trout fry need to reach a minimum of 30–35 mm TL by the onset of winter to allow recruitment to age 1 in temperature regimes like those of the streams we studied in the southern Rocky Mountains
note: Span 30-35 mm TL, stated as one minimum size at the onset of winter. It rests on the authors' laboratory study of Colorado River cutthroat (warm treatment, 974 GSDD: survival to the onset of winter more than 50%, fry averaging 34 mm TL; colder treatments, 763 and 666 GSDD: survival 18-35%, survivors averaging 26 and 25 mm TL; data rows 1107-1108) and on Peterson and Fausch (2002), where recruitment nearly always failed in two cold streams with fry averaging 26 and 30 mm TL by early September and occurred consistently in two warmer streams with fry of 45 and 69 mm TL by mid-September (pp. 1240-1241). The next sentence calls it a threshold 'we propose' whose validation and generalization among streams is still open. Table 4 (p. 1240) marks reaches where fry are likely to survive over winter as TL greater than 30 mm at the start of winter. Thorley and Branton (2022, p. 3) restate this sentence with their own fork-length conversion, 28-33 mm FL (data row 1109). Coded CRCT like this paper's other rows: the laboratory fish were Colorado River cutthroat and the field study held greenback and Colorado River cutthroat.

region: Laboratory and field, southern Rocky Mountains
quote: These observations and our own experimental results suggest that age-0 cutthroat trout fry must reach a threshold length of 30–35 mm to survive overwinter
note: Span 30-35 mm, stated as one threshold; the sentence names no length type. The paper's laboratory lengths are total lengths (Figure 5, p. 649, plots total lengths of living and dead fry, its shaded area 'the approximate minimum-size threshold for overwinter survival derived from previous field research (Peterson and Fausch 2002; Peterson et al. 2004)'), and the companion field paper states the same threshold as 30-35 mm TL (data row 1103). The 'observations' are Peterson and Fausch's September median lengths of age-0 trout: 26 and 30 mm in two cold streams (mean July 6.6 and 6.9 C) where annual electrofishing caught no age-0 and few age-1 trout, and 45 and 69 mm in two warmer streams (12.7 and 12.4 C) where age-1 fish were relatively abundant. The laboratory fish were Colorado River cutthroat; the field populations are named only as cutthroat trout.

quote: mortality during the recruitment bottleneck and through the first half of winter in our 2003 experiment was size dependent in the two colder temperature regimes, where mortality rates were highest
note: Size dependence held only in the colder regimes. Fry that died were smaller than living fry in the cold (F = 50.37; df = 2, 346; P < 0.0001) and intermediate regimes (F = 10.83; df = 2, 364; P < 0.0001) but not in the warm regime (F = 0.99; df = 2, 404; P = 0.37) (p. 647), and in the warm regime nearly all fry that survived to the onset of winter also survived to the end of the experiment (p. 650). A size cut-off is therefore a feature of cold regimes here, not a fixed requirement.

region: High-elevation streams, north-central Colorado, and laboratory
quote: The best-fitting model described TL of fish measured in the field and laboratory as an exponential function of accumulated degree-days from spawning to measurement
note: Degree-days are summed daily mean temperatures (p. 1234); base not stated. Window: spawning (field) or egg take (laboratory) to the time of measurement, not the growing season; substituting GSDD into the model gave predicted TL at the start of winter, from 23.1 mm in the coldest reach (581 GSDD) to 37.3 mm in the warmest (996 GSDD) (Table 4, p. 1240). The model also includes location (field or laboratory) and its interaction with degree-days, and was not clearly better than the same model without the interaction (delta AICc 0.45). The fitted equation is printed only in Figure 4 (p. 1240), not in the text. Laboratory fish were Colorado River cutthroat; the field reaches held greenback and Colorado River cutthroat.

quote: Colorado River cutthroat trout in laboratory streams was more than 50% to the onset of winter in a warm treatment (974 GSDD), where fry averaged 34 mm TL soon after the onset of winter
note: Mean TL of fry soon after the onset of winter in the warm laboratory treatment (974 GSDD), where survival to the onset of winter was more than 50%. The colder treatments are data row 1108. The laboratory paper (coleman_fausch2007ColdSummer) shows these means only in figures. One basis of the 30-35 mm TL threshold (data row 1103).

quote: compared with two colder treatments (763 and 666 GSDD), where survival was only 18–35% to the onset of winter and survivors averaged only 26 and 25 mm TL
note: Mean TL of the surviving fry in the two colder laboratory treatments, 26 mm at 763 GSDD and 25 mm at 666 GSDD (paired by order in the sentence), where survival to the onset of winter was only 18-35%. These are the lengths of the few survivors, not a requirement; compare the warm treatment, data row 1107. One basis of the 30-35 mm TL threshold (data row 1103).

region: Southern Rocky Mountains (Colorado); applied to Harmer and Grave creeks, Elk Valley, BC
quote: cutthroat trout fry need to reach a minimum of 30 - 35 mm TL ... 28 – 33 mm FL ... by the onset of winter to allow recruitment to age 1
note: Span 28-33 mm FL. The report quotes Coleman and Fausch's 30-35 mm TL threshold (data row 1103) and inserts its own fork-length conversion in square brackets, '[28 – 33 mm FL]'; the quote skips the opening and closing brackets with ellipses because the gate reads bracketed text as an editor's insert. The report applies the threshold to age-0 westslope cutthroat trout in the Harmer Creek and Grave Creek populations. It credits the sentence to Coleman and Fausch (2007a), which its reference list gives as the laboratory paper (TAFS 136:639); the sentence is in the field paper (TAFS 136:1231, p. 1241).

region: Upper Fording River, BC (applied to WCT)
quote: Age-0 fish from Ewin and LCO Dry Creeks were estimated to be less than 30 mm, suggesting poor overwintering survival
note: The report applies a 30 mm minimum, credited to Sogard (1997, a review of size-selective mortality in juvenile fishes) and both Coleman and Fausch (2007) papers, to its estimates of age-0 westslope cutthroat trout size in Ewin and LCO Dry creeks; the WCT values are estimated lengths, not a threshold measured on WCT. The sentence names no length type; the paragraph compares fry by fork length, whereas Coleman and Fausch state 30-35 mm TL (data row 1103).

region: Harmer and Grave creeks, Elk Valley, BC
quote: The model also estimated that expected fork length increased with GSDD from 35 (30-40 95% CI) mm at 800 GSDD to 43 (38-52 95% CI) mm at 1,200 GSDD
note: Expected fork length of age-0 WCT at the onset of winter, from the fork length submodel of the report's hierarchical Bayesian model (p. 20), printed as log(mu_L) = ((log(alpha_L0) + beta_GSDD (GSDD - 900) + alpha_L[p,y]) - alpha_EMERGE)(G + 1) + alpha_EMERGE, where G is the growth effect of dietary selenium and alpha_EMERGE the length at emergence. Estimates (Table 2, p. 24): alpha_L0, the expected fork length at the onset of winter at 900 GSDD, 36.6 mm (33-41.2 95% CL); beta_GSDD 0.000562 (7.23E-05 to 0.00125). GSDD follows Coleman and Fausch: from the beginning of the first week whose average exceeds and stays above 5 C to the last day of the first week averaging below 4 C (p. 4); base not stated. The report calls the relation less steep than Brooks and Robinson's (2022) for several Elk Valley streams (pp. 25-26). Model estimates, not observed lengths.

region: Harmer and Grave creeks, Elk Valley, BC
quote: The hBIN model estimated that the energetic status at the onset of winter was a strong positive predictor of the egg to age-1 survival
note: Energetic status is computed from fork length and body condition at the onset of winter (Equation 10, p. 17), and the log odds of egg-to-age-1 survival rise with its logarithm: beta_E 13.5 (3.15-33 95% CL); the survival of a 37.5 mm FL fish of average body condition, alpha_S0, is -3.66 (-4.4 to -2.79) on the log-odds scale (Table 2, p. 24). Energetic status explained 65% (29-85% 95% CI) of the 2017-2019 difference in recruitment between the Harmer Creek and Grave Creek populations, and the populations' difference in fork length fully explained their difference in energetic status; it explained 90% (76-96%) of the 2018 Harmer Creek Recruitment Failure, where body condition explained ~62% of the difference in energetic status and fork length ~38% (p. 29). The report gives no length threshold.

region: Harmer and Grave creeks, Elk Valley, BC
quote: The results also suggest that GSDD and dietary selenium explain 34% (4-58% 95% CI) and 8% (3-16% 95% CI) of the Reduced Recruitment, respectively
note: GSDD acts through fork length at the onset of winter: of the fork-length difference between the two populations, ~50% was explained by GSDD (p. 29). The Reduced Recruitment is the 2017-2019 difference in egg-to-age-1 survival between the Harmer Creek and Grave Creek populations; estimated GSDD was ~800 to ~900 in the Harmer Creek population (~1,000 in 2021) and ~1,050 to ~1,150 in the Grave Creek population area (just over 1,200 in 2021) (p. 25). GSDD did not explain the 2018 Recruitment Failure (p. ii). GSDD follows Coleman and Fausch (start: first week averaging above 5 C and staying above; end: last day of the first week averaging below 4 C; p. 4); base not stated.

region: Laboratory (Colorado River cutthroat trout); applied to Harmer and Grave creeks, Elk Valley, BC
quote: The model predicts that under controlled lab-based conditions overwinter survival of Cutthroat Trout fry is high (>90%) at a fork length greater than ~30 mm. Below 30 mm, survival decreases sharply
note: The report's own logistic regression of survival over the full overwintering period on fork length at the onset of winter, fitted to three points: the mean survival and mean fork length of fry in the warm, intermediate and cold laboratory treatments of Coleman and Fausch (p. 51). Printed (p. 52): Lab-based Overwinter Survival = e-5.21+0.239 x Fork Length / (1 + e-5.21+0.239 x Fork Length). At ~20 mm FL survival is predicted to be only 40% (p. 51); predictions below ~18 mm are unrealistic because WCT fry emerge around that size (Figure 19, p. 53). The report reasons that conditions in the wild (ice, predators, rapid temperature transitions, water quality) are likely more challenging, so the laboratory relation 'likely represents an overly conservative estimate of mortality in relation to fry size' (p. 53); the paragraph's first sentence says the reverse, that the laboratory mortality estimates are likely higher than would occur in the wild. Coleman and Fausch measured total length; the report does not say how the laboratory fork lengths were obtained (it converts TL to FL elsewhere with TL = 1.040 FL + 1.697, Mayhood 2012, p. 46). Applied to WCT in the Elk Valley.

region: Laboratory (Colorado River cutthroat trout); applied to Harmer and Grave creeks, Elk Valley, BC
quote: They estimated the following positive response between GSDD and fry survival to the onset of winter
note: Printed as: Fry survival to onset of winter = e-3.71 + 0.0048 x GSDD / (1 + e-3.71 + 0.0048 x GSDD), a logistic in GSDD with its exponents flattened (p. 49). Coleman and Fausch's field paper shows a logistic of survival to the onset of winter on GSDD fitted to their 2003 laboratory data as its Figure 3 (TAFS 136:1231, p. 1239), with no coefficients in the text, so these coefficients could not be checked there. Applied to Elk Valley temperature stations it predicts survival to the onset of winter of 29-38% in GRV-R3, 44-68% in HRM-R3 to HRM-R5, and 78-84% in HRM-R1, GRV-R1 and GRV-R2 (p. 49). GSDD sums average daily water temperature from when the weekly average exceeds 5 C to when it declines below 4 C (p. 12); base not stated.

region: Harmer and Grave creeks, Elk Valley, BC
quote: observed fry sizes in the Grave Creek and Harmer Creek population areas were similar to but slightly larger than predicted by the Coleman and Fausch models
note: Caution on transfer: the report predicts WCT fork length at the onset of winter from GSDD with Coleman and Fausch's Colorado relation converted to fork length (p. 46), and the same bullet says the response relationships with GSDD 'have not been specifically determined for WCT in the Elk Valley'. Observed WCT fry ran slightly larger than the Colorado relation predicts.

region: Inference from laboratory studies (a southern bull trout population; Arctic char)
quote: Together, these data suggest that bull trout require 1600 ATU from egg deposition to the onset of winter to increase their chance of survival during this season
note: Thermal units accumulate at 1 C for 24 h = 1 unit (p. 98), i.e. summed daily mean temperatures; base not stated. Window: egg deposition to the onset of winter, not Coleman and Fausch's growing season. The author's inference: 800 ATU for juveniles to emerge in laboratory studies of a southern bull trout population (Gould 1987; the same sentence gives 500 ATU for eggs to hatch), plus the additional 800 ATU after emergence at which juvenile survival of Arctic char (Salvelinus alpinus) is highest (Bebak et al. 2000). The post-emergence half is not measured on bull trout. The thesis's own northern streams hold self-sustaining juvenile bull trout populations with growing-season totals of 800 or less (data row 1118).

quote: All of the streams in the northern watershed where I describe thermal regimes have abundant, self-sustaining juvenile bull trout populations (Chapter 2), yet several of these streams accumulate very few thermal units throughout the growing season
note: Counter-evidence to applying a cutthroat-derived degree-day floor to bull trout. The sentence ends '(i.e., ≤ 800)'. Growing-season thermal units run from the estimated 50% egg hatch date to the onset of winter, defined on p. 101 as stream temperatures of 1.5 C or less for 7 consecutive days and in Table 3.2 (p. 127) as 2 C or less on two consecutive days; 1 C for 24 h = 1 unit, base not stated. Table 3.5 (p. 130) gives growing-season thermal units in the Northwest Territories streams of mean 651, range 378-936 (2013-2016). The author proposes local adaptation or countergradient growth.

quote: the size of age 0 + trout in autumn was dependent upon stream temperature during the incubation period
note: Steelhead and cutthroat trout pooled; same statement as data row 1120. Table 14 (p. 85) regresses the mean FL of age 0+ trout (steelhead and cutthroat) on September 30 in the lower 3.1 km of Carnation Creek on thermal summations of mean daily stream temperature at B-weir over 16 years: Mar. 1-May 31, r = 0.88, FL = 0.072(C) + 11.89; June 1-Sept. 30, r = 0.74, FL = 0.042(C) - 3.30; Mar. 1-Sept. 30 (total thermal history), r = 0.82, FL = 0.028(C) - 2.74; all P < 0.001. Base not stated. September FL was also negatively related to July trout numbers (r = -0.86). Survival of trout through winter was not determined (p. 89), so no size here is tied to survival.

quote: the size of age 0 + trout in autumn was dependent upon stream temperature during the incubation period
note: Steelhead and cutthroat trout pooled; same statement as data row 1119, where Table 14's equations are given (p. 85: FL of age 0+ trout on September 30 against Mar. 1-May 31 thermal summation, r = 0.88, FL = 0.072(C) + 11.89, 16 years). Base not stated. Survival of trout through winter was not determined (p. 89). Cutthroat alone: data row 1121.

region: Tributary-C and study section IX, Carnation Creek, Vancouver Island, BC
quote: September FL of age 0+ cutthroat trout was also correlated with stream temperature during their incubation period
note: Table 15 (p. 87) correlates the mean length of age 0+ cutthroat adjusted to September 30 with summed thermal history (CTU), 16 years (1972-1987): Tributary-C, Apr. 1-May 31 r = 0.70, P < 0.01, slope 0.114 (maximum CTU 508), June 1-Sept. 30 r = 0.64, P < 0.01, slope 0.063 (maximum 1523); study section IX, Apr.-May r = 0.75, P < 0.001, slope 0.061 (maximum 496), June-Sept. r = 0.70, P < 0.01, slope 0.044 (maximum 1581). Base not stated. Tributary-C was unlogged. Survival of trout through winter was not determined (p. 89).
